question: What is the main purpose of an autopilot?

options.text: To carry out the take-off in low visibility
To allow the aircraft to be flown with no crew on board
To relieve the pilot of physical and mental fatigue
To replace the flight director on the approach

explanation: Relieving the pilot of the fatigue of flying, especially on long flights, leaves the crew more alert for the critical landing phase.

question: Why can an autopilot fly a route more accurately than a human pilot?

options.text: It reacts more quickly to disturbances
It uses more powerful flight controls
It has a better view of the instruments

explanation: The autopilot detects and corrects disturbances faster than a human, so it holds the flight path more accurately.

question: Which phase of flight is not flown by the autopilot?
explanation: The autopilot does not carry out the take-off, which is flown by the pilot. It can be engaged shortly after take-off, at about 400 ft or even lower.

question: At about what height can the autopilot typically be engaged after take-off?
explanation: The autopilot can be engaged shortly after take-off, at about 400 ft or possibly lower, depending on the aircraft.

question: In a modern airliner with autothrottle, what moves the thrust levers?

options.text: The engine fuel control units alone, with no servos
Autothrottle servos, on commands from the thrust management computer

explanation: The autopilot flies the aircraft from attitude, navigation and pitot-static inputs; thrust is controlled by autothrottle servos commanded by the thrust management computer.

question: How long does a human pilot typically take just to detect a change of attitude?

options.text: About 50 milliseconds, the same as an autopilot

explanation: A human takes about 1/5 of a second (200 ms) to detect a change, then more time to decide which control to use. An autopilot detects and corrects in about 50 ms.

question: About how long does an autopilot take to detect a disturbance and apply a correction?
explanation: An autopilot detects a disturbance and applies the correction in about 50 ms, much quicker than a human pilot's 200 ms just to detect it.

question: How does an autopilot reduce crew workload?

options.text: It talks to ATC on the crew's behalf
It plans the route and files the flight plan with ATC
It monitors the engines and shuts them down
It flies the aircraft, freeing the crew for other tasks

explanation: Automatic systems flying the aircraft leave the crew more rested and free to concentrate on tasks such as navigation.

question: How is a single autopilot made fail-safe against a runaway?

options.text: By fitting a second autopilot on standby
By making its servos too weak to move the controls
By limiting actuator authority or rate of travel

explanation: Limiting the authority of the actuator, or the rate at which it can move, means the pilot can always override a malfunction and keep control.

question: What does "fail-safe" mean for a single autopilot?

options.text: The pilot can always override a malfunction
The autopilot continues working after a failure
The autopilot can complete a landing after a failure

explanation: A fail-safe autopilot is one whose malfunction can always be overridden by the pilot. The term applies to any single autopilot.

question: What is the key function of any autopilot?

options.text: Tracking VOR radials and localizer beams

explanation: Aircraft stabilisation is the key function, and all that some basic autopilots achieve. Modes such as VOR tracking and altitude hold are extras.

question: Which of these is a step in inner loop control?

options.text: Detecting that the aircraft has responded
Comparing the track made good with the flight plan track

explanation: Inner loop control senses the change, computes the correction, moves the controls with servomotors, detects that the aircraft has responded and re-centres the controls.

question: What is inner loop control also called?

options.text: Command mode control, or outer loop control

explanation: The inner loop is the innermost, closed loop that gives auto-stabilisation only.

question: Since aircraft are naturally stable, why fit a basic stabilising autopilot?

options.text: Aircraft are unstable in roll at all speeds and altitudes
It improves stability over a wider range of conditions
It is needed to make the controls lighter

explanation: Natural stability takes different forms and changes with conditions. The basic autopilot augments and fine-tunes it so that it is enhanced over a greater range of conditions.

question: About which point does the autopilot pitch and rotate the aircraft?

options.text: The aerodynamic centre of the tail

explanation: Like any control input, the autopilot's corrections manoeuvre the aircraft about its centre of gravity.

question: The autopilot is engaged with no mode selected. What does it provide?
explanation: With no outer loop mode selected only the inner loops work: the autopilot holds the attitude (stabilisation) and auto-trim relieves the pitch loads.

question: Which of these is an element of a closed loop control system?

options.text: A pre-set programme with no input

explanation: A closed loop has an input, an error detector or signal processor, an output, a control element and feedback.

question: What does an open loop control system lack?
explanation: An open loop system has no feedback; its controller may be a pre-set programme. If a human operator watches and corrects, the human closes the loop.

question: A heating system on a timer with no thermostat is an example of:
explanation: The pump runs for the set time whatever the room temperature, so there is no feedback. Adding a thermostat closes the loop.

question: What is a servomechanism?

options.text: A system with no feedback at all, driven by a timer or programme
A closed loop that turns a small input into a proportional larger output
A motor that turns at a constant speed
An open loop that holds a fixed output

explanation: A servomechanism is a closed loop control system in which a small input is converted into a larger output in strict proportion, as in powered flying controls.

question: In an autopilot inner loop, what senses a disturbance in one axis?

options.text: An accelerometer on the wing tip

explanation: A rate gyro senses disturbance of the aircraft about one axis only.

question: In an inner loop, what does the transducer do?

options.text: Converts the gyro's movement into an electrical signal
Converts electrical signals into movement of the control surfaces
Compares the input with the output

explanation: The transducer turns the mechanical movement of the gyro into an electrical signal for the signal processor.

question: What does the signal processor in an inner loop do?

options.text: It senses the disturbance in one axis
It converts the gyro's movement into a voltage for the servo
It finds the error and signals the servomotor

explanation: The signal processor, the error detector, compares the transducer signals with the input, works out the correction and sends a signal to the servomotor. It also takes position and rate feedback from the servomotor.

question: Which power sources can an autopilot servomotor use?

options.text: Mechanical springs only, wound by the pilot

explanation: The servomotor converts the processed signal into control movement in proportion to its rate and direction, using hydraulic, electrical or pneumatic power.

question: As the aircraft returns to its stabilised attitude, what happens to the control deflection?

options.text: It is progressively removed as the error falls
It reverses fully to stop the aircraft overshooting the attitude
It stays until the pilot resets it

explanation: The error signal from the transducer is progressively reduced, so the control deflection is removed once the disturbance has been corrected.

question: What do inner loop systems provide?

options.text: Speed control through the thrust levers

explanation: The inner loop is the innermost control loop and provides auto-stability only.

question: Which of these is an outer loop function?

options.text: Re-centring the ailerons after a gust

explanation: Outer loops are the extra facilities, such as altitude hold, heading hold, LNAV and VNAV. They act on the inner loop to manoeuvre the aircraft into the required position.

question: Which control channel of an autopilot drives the ailerons?
explanation: The roll channel controls the ailerons, the pitch channel the elevators, and the yaw channel the rudder.

question: About which axis does the roll channel control the aircraft?
explanation: Roll is about the longitudinal axis, pitch about the lateral axis and yaw about the normal (vertical) axis.

question: An aircraft has two autopilots, each controlling three axes. How many inner loops are there?
explanation: There is a separate inner loop for each axis of each autopilot: 2 autopilots × 3 axes = 6 inner loops.

question: A single axis autopilot normally controls which axis?
explanation: A single axis system is normally limited to the roll axis, the primary axis. At its most basic it just levels the wings.

question: Which is the secondary axis of an autopilot?
explanation: Roll is the primary axis, pitch the secondary axis and yaw the tertiary axis.

question: In a three-axis autopilot, to which channels are outer loop signals fed?

options.text: The pitch and yaw channels only

explanation: The roll and pitch channels are the primary control channels and receive the outer loop signals for the modes. The rudder channel is basically for stability.

question: Why is the rudder channel of an autopilot often linked to the roll channel?

options.text: To help coordinate turns and speed the stability response
To steer the aircraft on the runway
To allow heading changes without bank
To trim out an engine failure automatically with rudder trim

explanation: Interaction between the roll and rudder channels assists coordinated turns and gives a faster stability response.

question: How many autopilot axes are required for autoland?

options.text: None; autoland uses the flight director only

explanation: Three-axis control is required for autoland, because the rudder is needed to align the aircraft with the runway and control yaw on the roll-out.

question: For single pilot operation under IFR or at night, which autopilot is required at least?

options.text: One with VOR and ILS coupling and an autothrottle
One with altitude hold and heading mode
One with a yaw damper only

explanation: Single pilot IFR or night operation needs an autopilot with at least altitude hold and heading mode, which means at least a two-axis autopilot.

question: How must an autopilot be designed with respect to disengagement?

options.text: It must disengage automatically every hour for a trim check
It must need two switches to disengage
It must be quickly and positively disengaged
It must disengage only on the ground

explanation: Each system must be designed so that it can be disengaged quickly and positively, to stop it interfering with control of the aeroplane.

question: Where must the quick release autopilot controls be located?

options.text: On the centre console, beside the throttles, for both pilots
On both control wheels, on the side away from the throttles
On the mode control panel only
On the captain's control wheel only

explanation: Quick release controls must be on both control wheels, on the side of each wheel opposite the throttles.

question: If there is no automatic synchronising, what must the system provide?

options.text: An indication of actuator alignment with the controls
A manual trim wheel for each axis of the autopilot

explanation: Without automatic synchronising, the system must readily show the pilot how the actuating device is aligned relative to the control system it operates.

question: Which indication must an autopilot give the pilots?

options.text: The servo torque in each channel
The total time engaged on the flight
The current mode and any armed modes

explanation: Means must be provided to indicate the current mode of operation and any modes armed by the pilot.

question: What must an autopilot not produce, in normal operation or after a malfunction?

options.text: Hazardous loads or flight path deviations
Any control surface movement at all, in any axis

explanation: The system must be designed and adjusted so that it cannot produce hazardous loads or hazardous flight path deviations, in normal operation or after a malfunction.

question: Which of these is a type of autopilot actuator?
explanation: Actuators may be electromechanical, electrohydraulic or pneumatic.

question: How are autopilot actuators typically protected against excessive loads?

options.text: By sounding a warning but keeping the torque
By limiting servo torque and allowing slip or disengagement
By fusing every actuator at a fixed current
By locking the flight controls in place if a limit is reached

explanation: Torque applied by the servomotors is limited, and they can slip or disengage completely if the limits are exceeded.

question: What do autopilot interlocks do?

options.text: Prevent the pilot overriding the autopilot
Engage the autopilot automatically at 400 ft after take-off
Lock the controls when the autopilot is off
Allow and hold engagement only if valid signals are present

explanation: Interlocks, represented as relays in series, close to allow engagement and hold the autopilot engaged only while the inner loop components give valid signals.

question: What happens if a circuit monitored by an autopilot interlock fails?

options.text: The autopilot freezes the controls in place
The autopilot disengages with aural and visual warnings
Nothing happens; the interlock acts only before engagement

explanation: Failure of a monitored circuit causes disengagement with the associated aural and visual warnings, the same as operating the disengage switch.

question: In modern aircraft, how is interlock switching usually achieved?

options.text: By relays opened by the pilot before each engagement

explanation: The interlocks can be represented by relays in series, but in modern aircraft the switching is more likely solid state logic.

question: In a typical system, which conditions must be met before the autopilot can engage?

options.text: Both flight directors switched on and the gear retracted
No force on the control wheel; stab trim cut-out at NORMAL

explanation: Engagement in CMD or CWS is inhibited unless no force is being applied to the control wheel and the stabiliser trim autopilot cut-out switch is at NORMAL.

question: With the autopilot in CMD, the pilot applies control pressure. What happens?

options.text: It changes over to the other autopilot in CMD
It overrides into CWS in that axis

explanation: Control pressure applied after engagement in CMD overrides the autopilot into CWS pitch and/or roll; the CMD switch light stays on.

question: Which of these disengages the autopilot in a typical system?

options.text: Changing the selected heading on the MCP
Using either pilot's control wheel trim switch

explanation: The autopilot disengages for the disengage switch or bar, a trim switch, the stab trim cut-out, TO/GA in certain cases, loss of hydraulics, an IRS failure, EFI transfer or loss of a needed sensor.

question: In a typical system, when does pressing TO/GA disengage a single autopilot?

options.text: At any height above 2000 ft RA
When engaged in CWS or CMD below 2000 ft RA
Only on the ground, before the take-off roll begins

explanation: Pressing either TOGA switch with a single autopilot engaged below 2000 ft RA disconnects it, as does TOGA after touchdown with both autopilots in CMD.

question: When can two autopilots be engaged at the same time in a typical system?

options.text: Only on the ground, for the preflight test
Only when approach mode is engaged

explanation: Only one autopilot can be engaged at a time unless APP mode is engaged. Engaging the second otherwise disengages the first.

question: An autopilot is engaged in CMD while the FD commands are more than half scale from centre. What happens?

options.text: It engages in CWS and the FD bars retract
It engages and centres the bars by banking
It engages in CMD and follows the bars

explanation: With FD pitch or roll commands more than ½ scale off centre, the autopilot engages in CWS for that axis and the command bars retract.

question: Why must the autopilot be synchronised before it takes over?

options.text: To align it with true north
To take control smoothly without snatching the controls
To match its internal clock with the FMS clock

explanation: The aircraft must be trimmed and the autopilot synchronised to the existing attitude, so that engagement is smooth and does not snatch the controls.

question: How do synchronising circuits work?

options.text: They hold the controls firmly until the pilot lets go of them
They wash out standing signals in pitch and roll to zero
They add a fixed signal to each channel

explanation: Synchronising circuits sense standing signals in the pitch and roll channels and wash them out to zero, so the servo stops in step with the datum attitude. The trim indicator returns to centre.

question: What is the purpose of a trim system?

options.text: To relieve control forces while holding the attitude
To change the aircraft's attitude rapidly
To limit the control deflection available at high speed

explanation: Trim relieves the pilot of forces on the controls while the aircraft attitude is maintained.

question: On larger aircraft, how is manual trim usually provided, particularly in pitch?

options.text: By moving the CG with fuel
By mechanical trim tabs only, exactly as on light aircraft
By electrical actuators that bias the PFCU or stabiliser

explanation: Light aircraft use mechanical linkages to trim tabs; larger aircraft use electrical actuators that bias the powered flying control units, especially for pitch.

question: Why does manual pitch trim operation usually disconnect the autopilot?

options.text: The trim switch is wired to the disengage circuit by law in all aircraft
The autopilot cannot coordinate with manual trim movement
Manual trim overloads the autopilot servos
The autopilot would trim the opposite way

explanation: The autopilot cannot coordinate manual trim movement with CG or aerodynamic changes, so manual pitch trim normally disconnects it.

question: Without auto-trim, what problem arises when an autopilot holding an out-of-trim force is disconnected?

options.text: The aircraft stays perfectly in trim

explanation: The autopilot holds the force with its servos; on disconnect that standing load is released and the aircraft lurches in an unknown direction. The held load also adds drag.

question: In which axis is automatic trim available with the autopilot engaged?
explanation: With the autopilot engaged, automatic trim is available only in pitch: automatic pitch trim, or auto-trim.

question: When is auto-trim active?

options.text: Only when the autopilot is engaged
Only when the pilot holds the trim switch

explanation: Auto-trim is active only with the autopilot engaged. Fly-by-wire arrangements differ.

question: On modern jet transports, what does the auto-trim servo usually move?

options.text: The aileron trim tab on each wing

explanation: It operates either the trim tab or, more commonly on modern jets, the variable incidence stabiliser, which keeps the elevator neutral relative to the stabiliser.

question: Why is trimming with a variable incidence stabiliser an advantage for the autopilot?

options.text: It allows the autopilot to fly without any hydraulic power
It keeps full elevator authority both ways from trim
It removes the need for an elevator

explanation: With the elevator kept neutral relative to the stabiliser, the autopilot has full elevator authority either side of the trimmed position, and the aircraft is in trim if the autopilot disconnects.

question: Which is one method of sensing an out-of-trim condition for auto-trim?

options.text: The airspeed trend vector on the PFD
The standing load on the actuator

explanation: Either the standing load on an electrical actuator or the actuator's displacement gives the size and direction of the out-of-trim force.

question: What happens if the auto-trim system fails?

options.text: Warnings appear and the autopilot disengages
The aircraft is trimmed fully nose down
The autopilot continues and the crew trims manually with it engaged

explanation: A trim failure gives warning lights or display indications and the autopilot disengages with visual and aural alerts. An excessive trim input, such as a runaway, can also trigger the alert.

question: Without auto-trim, what procedure reduces the snatch on autopilot disconnection?

options.text: Engage the autopilot only in CWS
Hold the trim switch while disengaging
Keep the autopilot engaged until touchdown, then disconnect it

explanation: The operating procedure sets a time after which the autopilot is disengaged, the aircraft re-trimmed and the autopilot re-engaged.

question: Which indication is always provided with auto-trim?

options.text: A digital read-out of elevator angle
A stabiliser trim indicator and an auto-trim fail warning
An aural call of each trim movement
A green light on the throttle quadrant for each trim movement

explanation: With auto-trim there is always a stabiliser trim indicator and an auto-trim failure warning so that the system can be monitored.

question: Where is the mode control panel usually located?
explanation: The MCP is on the glareshield and is the pilot's interface with the auto-flight system: engaging autopilots and selecting pitch and roll modes.

question: How many command modes can be engaged in one channel at once?
explanation: Only one command mode may be engaged in a single channel at a time: one in roll and one in pitch.

question: Why can the autopilot not hold both speed and altitude by pitch alone?

options.text: Speed and altitude are both roll modes
The air data computer cannot supply both
Holding both together would overstress the aircraft structure
Only one pitch mode can be engaged; thrust is needed for the other

explanation: Pitch can hold one target. With an autothrottle the autopilot can hold altitude while the autothrottle holds speed.

question: In auto-flight terms, what does "capture" mainly refer to?

options.text: Intercepting a radio beam, such as the glide slope
Holding a selected altitude or heading

explanation: "Hold" means maintaining a value, as in altitude hold. "Capture" relates mainly to intercepting beams from ground aids, as in glide slope capture.

question: What does a beam sensor do?

options.text: Switches modes automatically on flying into a beam
Displays the beam on the HSI

explanation: The beam sensor detects beam deviation and switches from the intercept mode to beam tracking automatically, for example from altitude hold to glide slope track.

question: Which of these is a roll channel outer loop mode?
explanation: Roll channel modes include heading hold and select, VOR and LOC intercept and track, and LNAV. Altitude, speed, Mach, V/S and VNAV are pitch modes.

question: Which of these is a pitch channel outer loop mode?
explanation: Pitch channel modes include altitude hold, speed hold, Mach hold, vertical speed and VNAV.

question: Which autopilot channel uses manometric (air) data for its outer loop modes?
explanation: Altitude, airspeed, Mach and vertical speed give the current status for outer loop control in the pitch channel.

question: What supplies attitude reference to the auto-flight computer?

options.text: A vertical and directional gyro, an INS or an IRS

explanation: Depending on the age of the aircraft, roll, pitch and yaw come from a vertical gyro and directional gyro pair, an INS or an IRS. These may also feed the ADI and HSI.

question: What does a magnetic heading reference system combine?

options.text: GPS track corrected with magnetic variation only
Inertial heading with magnetic compass heading

explanation: An MHRS, or gyro-magnetic compass, combines inertial heading with magnetic heading, giving magnetic heading to the HSI and the auto-flight computer.

question: When does HDG SEL disengage automatically?

options.text: When the aircraft reaches the selected heading and rolls level
On capture of the selected course in VOR LOC or APP
When a new heading is set on the MCP
When the autopilot is in CWS

explanation: Heading select disengages automatically when the selected radio course is captured in VOR LOC or APP mode.

question: Which localizer course does the LOC mode track?

options.text: The localizer of the reciprocal runway

explanation: LOC mode captures and tracks the localizer along the inbound front course. Back-course tracking is not available.

question: Pressing VOR LOC with a localizer frequency tuned selects:
explanation: The switch selects VOR mode with a VOR frequency tuned and LOC mode with a localizer frequency tuned. VOR LOC armed is annunciated.

question: What does the capture point of a VOR or LOC course depend on?

options.text: The selected heading on the MCP only
The intercept angle and the closure rate

explanation: The capture point varies with intercept angle and closure rate. Localizer capture occurs not later than ½ dot deviation.

question: Localizer capture occurs not later than:
explanation: The localizer is captured no later than ½ dot deviation, after which the roll commands track it.

question: What is the VOR "cone of confusion"?

options.text: The area where radials are widely spaced
The area beyond the VOR's range
The area where two VOR stations share the same frequency
An area overhead the VOR where signals are unusable

explanation: Overhead the beacon the signals are unusable, so for a time depending on ground speed and height the aircraft receives no usable guidance.

question: Approaching a VOR, why does the CDI become more sensitive?

options.text: The radials converge towards the station
The VOR switches to a narrower beam close to the station

explanation: The radials converge on the station, so a given distance off track becomes a larger angle and the indication more sensitive, until it becomes unusable.

question: How does the autopilot fly through the VOR cone of confusion?

options.text: It changes to HDG SEL on the heading set on the MCP
It holds the drift-corrected heading, then reverts to VOR
It continues tracking the last radial signal
It disconnects and alerts the pilot

explanation: Over-station sensing de-couples the roll channel from the beam. The autopilot holds the drift-corrected heading for a set time, then returns to VOR mode. It does not go into heading select.

question: Without an FMS, how could an older aircraft follow INS waypoints automatically?

options.text: By using the VOR mode with the INS tuned on the radio panel
By coupling the INS or IRS to the autopilot

explanation: Older aircraft may couple the INS/IRS to the autopilot to steer sequentially through waypoints loaded before flight.

question: In heading select, how does the autopilot set the bank angle?

options.text: Always 30° of bank, whatever the heading change required
In proportion to TAS, with no limit
In proportion to the heading error, up to a set maximum

explanation: The roll command is proportional to the deviation from the selected heading, limited to a maximum bank angle.

question: In LNAV mode, what controls the autopilot's roll?

options.text: The FMC, to intercept and track the active route
The heading selected on the MCP
The VOR tuned on the radio panel for the route

explanation: In LNAV the FMC controls the roll to intercept and track the active route, which can include SIDs, STARs and instrument approaches.

question: Which is an LNAV engagement requirement?

options.text: An active route in the FMC

explanation: LNAV needs an active FMC route, the capture criteria satisfied, and the LNAV switch pressed.

question: Within what distance of the active route segment are the LNAV capture criteria met in any case?
explanation: Any aircraft within 3 NM of the active route segment satisfies the capture criteria. Beyond that it must be on an intercept course of 90° or less that meets the leg before the active waypoint.

question: Outside 3 NM of the route, which intercept condition allows LNAV capture?

options.text: Any intercept angle, provided it is after the active waypoint
An intercept of 90° or less, before the active waypoint
An intercept of 45° or less only
A heading directly towards the active waypoint

explanation: Outside 3 NM the aircraft must be on an intercept course of 90° or less and must meet the active segment before the active waypoint.

question: Which of these causes LNAV to disconnect?

options.text: Passing a waypoint in the route

explanation: LNAV disconnects at the end of the active route or a discontinuity, on intercepting or missing an approach inbound track, on loss of capture criteria or on selecting HDG SEL.

question: Which altitude does ALT HOLD hold when the switch is pressed away from the MCP altitude?

options.text: The cruise altitude in the FMC
The radio altitude at the moment the switch was pressed
The barometric altitude at the moment it was pressed

explanation: ALT HOLD holds either the MCP altitude or the uncorrected barometric altitude at which the switch was pressed. Away from the MCP altitude the switch light stays on.

question: How is ALT HOLD at the MCP selected altitude annunciated?

options.text: ALT HOLD, with the ALT HOLD switch light on
ALT ACQ, with the switch light out
ALT HOLD, with the switch light out

explanation: At the MCP altitude, ALT HOLD is annunciated with the switch light extinguished. Not at the MCP altitude, the switch light stays illuminated.

question: When is ALT HOLD inhibited?

options.text: Whenever the autothrottle is in N1

explanation: ALT HOLD is inhibited after glide slope capture, because the pitch channel is then following the glide slope.

question: To which altimeter setting is the MCP altitude referenced for autopilot "A"?
explanation: Autopilot A and its FD use the captain's barometric setting; autopilot B uses the first officer's. Once ALT HOLD engages, changing the setting does not move the selected altitude.

question: What is the altitude acquire (ALT ACQ) mode?

options.text: The transition from a climb or descent onto the MCP altitude
A mode that captures the glide slope from above
A mode that sets the altimeter automatically
A mode that holds the altitude reached after a go-around

explanation: ALT ACQ is entered automatically from V/S, LVL CHG or VNAV to level off at the MCP altitude. It is also armed when climbing or descending in CWS.

question: When levelling off in VNAV, what pitch mode is annunciated during altitude acquire?
explanation: In V/S or LVL CHG, ALT ACQ is annunciated during level-off. In VNAV, VNAV stays annunciated throughout the altitude acquire.

question: How does the IAS/Mach hold mode control speed?

options.text: By pitching the aircraft up or down
By extending the speed brakes automatically

explanation: It compares the selected speed with the ADC value and pitches up to reduce speed or down to increase it.

question: In V/S mode, what does the autothrottle do?

options.text: It holds a fixed N1 set by the crew
It holds the selected airspeed in SPEED mode

explanation: V/S gives pitch commands to hold the vertical speed and engages the autothrottle in SPEED mode to hold the selected airspeed.

question: In ALT HOLD at the selected altitude, a new MCP altitude more than 100 ft away is set. What happens to V/S?

options.text: It engages at the last vertical speed used
It becomes armed, engaged by the thumbwheel
It stays unavailable until ALT HOLD is cancelled

explanation: V/S becomes armed and can be engaged by moving the vertical speed thumbwheel.

question: In LVL CHG, what controls the speed during a climb?

options.text: Pitch, with the autothrottle in N1
Thrust, with pitch holding a fixed rate
The FMC, through the VNAV path
Pitch, with the autothrottle in SPEED

explanation: LVL CHG coordinates pitch and thrust: in a climb pitch holds the MCP speed while the autothrottle sets N1 (climb thrust).

question: During a LVL CHG descent, what does the autothrottle annunciate while reducing thrust?

options.text: SPEED, then RETARD at the aft stop

explanation: During the descent pitch is MCP SPD and the autothrottle shows RETARD as it reduces thrust; at idle it shows ARM.

question: LVL CHG is engaged with no active speed mode. What becomes the target speed?
explanation: The IAS/Mach display and speed cursors synchronise to the existing speed, which becomes the target. It can then be changed with the MCP speed selector.

question: In VNAV, what commands the autopilot pitch and autothrottle?

options.text: The FMC, flying the CDU vertical profile
The MCP speed and vertical speed selectors only

explanation: With VNAV engaged, the FMC commands AFDS pitch and autothrottle modes to fly the vertical profile set on the CDUs.

question: Which condition must be met before VNAV can be engaged?

options.text: The flight directors switched off for the climb

explanation: Pressing VNAV selects the mode provided the FMC performance initialisation is complete. The MCP speed display then blanks.

question: Which pitch modes may be annunciated in VNAV?

options.text: ALT HOLD or ALT ACQ only

explanation: The FMA shows VNAV SPD or VNAV PTH for pitch and FMC SPD, N1, RETARD or ARM for the autothrottle.

question: What constrains VNAV climbs and descents?
explanation: VNAV climbs and descents stop at the selected MCP altitude. VNAV speeds can be changed on the CDU.

question: In VNAV path cruise, the crew selects a lower MCP altitude. What happens?

options.text: Descent is armed to begin at the top of descent
Nothing until the crew presses LVL CHG
Descent starts immediately at idle thrust in LVL CHG

explanation: Selecting a lower MCP altitude in cruise arms the FMC to begin the descent automatically at the calculated top of descent point.

question: With CWS engaged, how does the autopilot respond to control pressure?

options.text: It ignores the pressure and holds the existing attitude
It manoeuvres the aircraft as the pilot pushes

explanation: In CWS the autopilot manoeuvres the aeroplane in response to control pressure similar to manual flight; when the pressure is released it holds the attitude.

question: In CWS, aileron pressure is released at 5° of bank. What does the autopilot do?

options.text: Rolls wings level and holds the heading

explanation: If pressure is released with 6° or less of bank, the autopilot rolls wings level and holds the existing heading, except in certain conditions.

question: When is the CWS wings-level heading hold feature inhibited?

options.text: Below 1500 ft RA with the gear down
With the autothrottle engaged in speed mode
In the cruise with LNAV armed

explanation: It is inhibited below 1500 ft RA with gear down, after FD VOR capture at TAS of 250 kt or less, and after FD LOC capture in APP mode.

question: When does the pitch axis engage in CWS with CMD selected?

options.text: When the aircraft is below 1000 ft radio altitude
When no command pitch mode is selected
When a roll mode is selected

explanation: Pitch goes to CWS P when no command pitch mode is selected (or one is deselected), or when the pilot overrides the autopilot pitch with column force.

question: In ALT HOLD, the pilot overrides pitch and releases within 250 ft of the selected altitude. What happens?

options.text: V/S engages at the current rate
The autopilot holds the new altitude it has reached
CWS P changes to ALT ACQ, then ALT HOLD

explanation: Released within 250 ft, CWS P changes to ALT ACQ and the autopilot returns to the selected altitude. Held beyond 250 ft, pitch stays in CWS P.

question: How can CWS R be used to intercept a radio course?

options.text: Select HDG SEL first, then CWS R
Steer onto it with VOR/LOC or APP armed
Hold the wheel until the course is centred
It cannot; CWS R disarms VOR/LOC

explanation: With VOR/LOC or APP armed, CWS R can be used to steer to the course; on intercept the annunciation changes from CWS R to VOR/LOC and the autopilot tracks it.

question: How does touch control steering differ from CWS?

options.text: The autopilot servos are disengaged while the button is held
The autopilot manoeuvres the aircraft through its own servos while the button is held
It works only in the roll axis

explanation: In TCS the channels and servos are disengaged while the button is held and the pilot flies manually. Releasing it re-engages the autopilot, which holds the attitude left.

question: What indicates that an autopilot has disengaged?

options.text: A message on the FMS control unit only
A green A/P light on the MCP
A flashing red A/P light and a tone

explanation: The A/P light flashes red and a tone sounds. Either disengage light or switch resets the warning.

question: When does the A/P warning light stay steady red?

options.text: Stabiliser out of trim below 800 ft on a dual approach
After a normal disengagement by the crew

explanation: A steady red light shows, for example, a stabiliser out of trim below 800 ft RA on a dual channel approach, ALT ACQ inhibited in an A/P go-around, the red test or a ground test failure.

question: What does a flashing amber A/P light indicate?

options.text: An automatic reversion to CWS in pitch or roll
A complete failure of both autopilots

explanation: The light flashes amber if the autopilot automatically reverts to CWS pitch or roll while in CMD. Pressing the light or engaging another mode resets it.

question: What are typical maximum pitch and bank angles in normal autopilot operation?
explanation: Typical limits are ±10° pitch and ±30° roll. They are not fixed by law and vary between aircraft.

question: What is gain adaption in an autopilot?

options.text: Changing the system's response to suit the flight condition
Reducing the pitch limits of the autopilot at high altitude

explanation: Altitude, speed, load, configuration and rate of manoeuvre change the handling. Gain adaption alters the system's response to a given signal, like changing gear ratios, mainly with IAS.

question: How is redundancy achieved in an integrated flight management and guidance system?

options.text: By a single, very reliable computer
By manual back-up of every function
By two or more systems of each type

explanation: Each subsystem is duplicated or triplicated, so the failure of one does not affect the operation of the complete system.

question: Why is a Mach trim system fitted to some jet aircraft?

options.text: To counter Mach tuck as the centre of pressure moves aft
To counter the nose-up pitch as the centre of pressure moves forward
To control the aircraft in roll at high Mach
To trim the rudder at high Mach number

explanation: At high Mach the shock waves move the centre of pressure aft and the nose tends to drop. Mach trim adds nose-up trim automatically as Mach number increases.

question: Through which control does a Mach trim system act?
explanation: Mach trim acts in pitch, applying nose-up inputs through the elevator or, more commonly, the horizontal stabiliser.
